The M2 catalyst with metal-modified acid sites demonstrated enhanced olefin selectivity compared to conventional H/ZSM-5, validating the acid site engineering approach for product slate optimization. This capability enables targeting specific product distributions based on market demands or downstream processing requirements. Beyond the primary SOPO objectives, Task 4 developed an innovative hydroformylation approach for converting olefin-rich pyrolysis oils into higher-value aldehydes and alcohols suitable for surfactant production. This work demonstrates potential for value-added chemical production rather than conventional recycling back to steam crackers. Comparative studies revealed rhodium catalysts exhibit 104 times higher activity than cobalt for straight-chain olefin hydroformylation under comparable conditions. Modified rhodium catalysts with BIPHEPHOS ligands (3:1 molar ratio with rhodium precursor) achieved 94% regioselectivity for terminal aldehyde formation from C10-C14 PCR-HDPE pyrolysis oil. This exceptional selectivity was confirmed through ¹H NMR analysis of the aldehyde alpha-carbon region, distinguishing between terminal and internal isomers. Temperature sensitivity analysis demonstrated rhodium selectivity decreased from 94% at 120°C to lower values at 90°C, attributed to reduced catalyst-ligand complexation at lower temperatures. Phosphorus NMR studies are planned to confirm this mechanism. Substrate concentration effects showed that while high concentrations reduced selectivity at fixed catalyst loading, increasing rhodium concentration restored both activity and selectivity. At substrate-to-catalyst ratio of 6000, rhodium maintained notable conversion with cobalt-comparable selectivity, demonstrating robustness with complex plastic oil feedstocks. A continuous flow hydrogenation reactor was constructed using 10 wt% palladium on alumina catalyst to convert aldehydes to alcohols. While initial conversion rates require optimization through adjustment of pressure, temperature, catalyst selection, and flow rate verification, the system successfully demonstrated proof-of- concept for integrated hydroformylation-hydrogenation processing. This two-step approach transforms pyrolysis oil olefins into surfactant-grade alcohols, representing a significant value addition compared to conventional plastic waste processing. Model pyrolysis oil studies using 46 wt% 1-hexene, 24 wt% heptane, and 30 wt% toluene (mimicking C8-C11 PCR-HDPE cuts) confirmed the necessity of either increased catalyst loading or substrate dilution to maintain high selectivity. These findings guide scale-up strategies for industrial application. This project developed and validated both fixed-bed and fluidized-bed reactor systems for catalytic upgrading. The fixed-bed reactor provided precise control for fundamental studies and achieved excellent performance during the 100-hour demonstration. A fluidized-bed reactor system was constructed and commissioned during the program to enable better mixing and scalability for processing whole fractions of plastic pyrolysis products. Comparative testing between reactor configurations was planned to evaluate performance trade-offs for different feedstock compositions and throughput requirements. Both reactor systems incorporated online and offline analytical capabilities. The fixed-bed system utilized online GC with heated transfer lines for real-time monitoring, while ice- cooled condensers enabled collection and offline analysis of heavy products. This dual analytical approach provided comprehensive material balance closure and product distribution characterization. The analytical methodologies developed during this program provide a robust foundation for future scale-up activities. Topic Area 5 – Solvent Targeted Recovery and Precipitation (STRAP) of Plastic Wastes Task 2.5: Development of STRAP process for rigid PIW films focused on the development of computational and experimental methods to apply STRAP to rigid post-industrial waste (PIW) films.
